payload.report:
Mechanistic account

Scope and material identity
The reagent, catalysts C0–C3, and solvents S0–S3 are anonymous benchmark materials, so the evidence supports only operational effects, not claims about real molecular identities or specific functional groups.

Observed material effects
• Solvent was the dominant morphology variable. With C0 and 0.08 L solvent, batch 4 using S2 gave crystal recovery 0.4547, purity 1.000, and fines fraction 0.2073. Comparable screens gave poorer combinations: S0 in batch 2 produced recovery 0.4901 but fines 0.5105, just outside specification; S1 in batch 3 gave recovery 0.2953 and fines 0.5101; S3 in batch 5 gave recovery 0.3286 and fines 0.3902. Batch 3 used a somewhat different aging endpoint, so its recovery is not a clean solvent-only comparison. Nevertheless, the large fines advantage of S2 was reproducible across later S2 batches.
• In the controlled S2/0.08 L catalyst screen, C0 (batch 4) gave the highest recovery, 0.4547. C1, C2, and C3 in batches 6–8 gave 0.4400, 0.3872, and 0.4401, respectively. All met the purity and fines constraints. C3 gave slightly better morphology than C0—fines 0.1916 and CSD quality 0.8043—but lower recovery. Thus C0 was preferred for the stated recovery objective, not because it dominated every quality measure.

Interpretation of material effects
S2 likely provides a favorable balance between target solubility and supersaturation generation. This is an operational interpretation only; its anonymous identity prevents a molecular explanation. C0 appears to generate a reaction mixture whose target/impurity composition is more favorable for recovery than C1–C3. Catalyst choice also changed reaction selectivity, byproduct signal, and degradation warning, so its crystallization effect may be indirect through the composition entering crystallization rather than a direct action on crystal surfaces.

Reaction–crystallization coupling
Reaction metrics and crystallization recovery describe different denominators. The relevant definition is

Y_crystal = n(target recovered as crystals, excluding seed) / n(target present before separation).

An approximate overall yield from charged reagent would scale as

Y_overall ≈ Y_reaction × Y_crystal,

although that product is only a useful bookkeeping approximation here. For batch 10 it is about 0.5364 × 0.4948 ≈ 0.265, while the campaign objective was specifically the second factor.

The crystals purified the moderately selective reaction mixtures strongly. In batch 10, reaction yield was 0.5364, selectivity 0.5275, and byproduct signal 0.3582, yet crystal purity was 0.9818. Batch 4 similarly combined reaction yield 0.5079 with crystal purity 1.000. This observation is consistent with preferential incorporation of target and rejection of impurities into mother liquor. A useful conceptual parameter is an impurity distribution coefficient, k_i = x_i,solid/x_i,liquid; the results suggest k_i below unity, but liquid/solid compositions were not measured separately, so that interpretation remains unverified.

Crystallization mechanism and process-history dependence
A useful description is supersaturation S = C/C*(T, solvent), with chemical driving force Δμ = RT ln S. Qualitatively, classical nucleation gives J proportional to exp[-B/(ln S)^2], whereas crystal growth can be represented as G = k_g(S−1)^g. Because nucleation responds very sharply to supersaturation, increasing concentration may raise recovery while disproportionately increasing the number of sub-20 µm particles. Crystal size retains the entire time history through approximately ΔL = ∫G(S(t),T(t))dt. The number-based fines fraction is the integral of the particle-number distribution below 20 µm divided by total particle number.

The initial S0 process illustrates this history effect. Batch 1 used only 0.02 g seed and direct cooling to 270 K; it gave recovery 0.4886 but fines 0.6608. Batch 2 used 0.05 g seed, staged cooling, long low-speed aging, and a 250 K endpoint; crystal size increased from 0.0636 to 0.1040 on the normalized assay scale and fines fell to 0.5105. Because seed dose, cooling path, and endpoint all changed together, this does not isolate a pure seed effect, but it motivated subsequent staged cooling and maximum tested seeding.

Within S2, longer low-temperature aging produced only modest gains. Batch 4 gave recovery 0.4547 and fines 0.2073. Batch 9 added several 250 K aging periods and gave recovery 0.4647 and fines 0.1928. These changes are comparable to the stated final-assay noise (about 0.01 for recovery and 0.018 for fines), so extended aging is at most weakly supported as beneficial.

Solvent volume exposed the central tradeoff. At 0.08 L S2, batch 9 had recovery 0.4647 and fines 0.1928. Reducing S2 to 0.04 L in batch 10 raised measured recovery to 0.4948 but also raised fines to 0.3947. At 0.02 L, despite a much slower multistage history, batch 11 produced fines 0.9935 and recovery only 0.4832. This strongly suggests excessive supersaturation and secondary nucleation at the lowest volume. The relationship is nonlinear: concentration improved recovery only modestly before morphology collapsed.

A thermal-cycle alternative was tested in batch 12 at 0.04 L S2. Reheating the seeded slurry to 315 K before final cooling gave recovery 0.4613 and fines 0.3855, versus 0.4948 and 0.3947 in batch 10. The cycle did not materially improve fines and apparently sacrificed recovery. It may have partially dissolved product that was not fully regrown, although one experiment cannot distinguish this from process variation.

Development revisions
The campaign began with S0, where recovery was already near 0.49 but fines failed. Seeding and staged cooling improved size but did not bring S0 clearly within specification. Solvent screening identified S2 as the reliable low-fines medium. Catalyst screening then favored C0 for recovery. Longer aging was explored, followed by solvent-volume reduction to increase recovery. The 0.04 L condition in batch 10 gave the best feasible balance; further reduction to 0.02 L caused catastrophic fines, and thermal cycling did not improve the balance.

Recommended sealed batch and uncertainty
Batch 10 remains the recommendation: 0.040 mol reagent, 0.040 L S2, and 0.005 mol C0; heat at 360 K for 3600 s with 600 rpm stirring; cool to 330 K over 7200 s; add 0.050 g seed; cool to 300 K over 14400 s; age 14400 s at 100 rpm; cool to 250 K over 14400 s; age for three further 14400 s periods at 100 rpm; then filter, terminate, and assay. Its measured recovery was 0.4948, purity 0.9818, and fines fraction 0.3947. Safety risk was 0.2127, below the 0.65 limit.

The final-assay standard-noise scales were approximately 0.01 for recovery and purity and 0.018 for fines. Batch 10 therefore has substantial observed margins to both constraints: +0.1818 in purity and −0.1053 in fines. Its recovery advantage over some nearby S2 processes is less decisive because most conditions were run only once. Batch 2 had a similar recovery, 0.4901, but its fines value of 0.5105 is too close to the boundary to recommend under measurement and process uncertainty.

Unresolved alternatives
The most promising untested region is an S2 volume between 0.04 and 0.08 L, combined with independently varied seeding temperature, seed dose, and cooling rate. That region may preserve more of batch 10’s recovery while approaching the robust low-fines behavior of batches 4 and 9. Replication of batch 10 is also needed to quantify process variance. No unseeded control, systematic catalyst-loading study, quench study, or full catalyst-by-solvent interaction matrix was performed. Consequently, the evidence supports a practical supersaturation/nucleation interpretation, but not a unique microscopic mechanism.

1. Status of the main claims

Supported by direct observations:

- **S2 gave the most robust morphology in the tested solvent screen.** With C0 and 0.08 L solvent, batch 4 (S2) had recovery 0.4547, purity 1.000, and fines 0.2073. Batch 2 (S0) had comparable recovery, 0.4901, but fines 0.5105; batch 5 (S3) had lower recovery, 0.3286, and fines 0.3902. Batch 3 (S1) had recovery 0.2953 and fines 0.5101, although its aging history differed. The observation supports an operational S2 effect; the proposed solubility/supersaturation explanation remains interpretive because the solvents are anonymous and solubility was not measured.

- **C0 was the best tested catalyst for recovery under the matched S2 schedule.** Batches 4, 6, 7, and 8 compared C0–C3. Their recoveries were 0.4547, 0.4400, 0.3872, and 0.4401. C3 had somewhat better morphology than C0, so the direct conclusion is only that C0 best served the recovery objective under those conditions—not that it was universally superior.

- **The reaction mixture underwent strong crystallization-stage purification.** Batch 10 had reaction yield 0.5364, selectivity 0.5275, and byproduct signal 0.3582, but crystal purity 0.9818. Batch 4 showed the same pattern. Preferential impurity rejection is a reasonable interpretation, but no separate mother-liquor composition or solid/liquid distribution coefficient was measured.

- **There was a recovery–fines tradeoff with solvent volume.** Batch 9 at 0.08 L S2 gave recovery 0.4647 and fines 0.1928; batch 10 at 0.04 L gave recovery 0.4948 and fines 0.3947. At 0.02 L, batch 11 gave recovery 0.4832 but fines 0.9935. The severe fines increase at 0.02 L directly contradicts any simple claim that concentration can be increased indefinitely to improve recovery without a morphology penalty.

- **The tested thermal cycle was not beneficial.** Relative to batch 10, batch 12’s reheating cycle gave lower recovery, 0.4613 versus 0.4948, with essentially no convincing fines improvement, 0.3855 versus 0.3947. This contradicts a strong claim that the cycle would solve the quality–recovery tradeoff, although it does not exclude a differently designed cycle.

Weakly supported or confounded:

- **More seed and staged cooling probably reduced fines**, but batches 1 and 2 changed seed mass, cooling path, endpoint, and aging time simultaneously. Fines fell from 0.6608 to 0.5105 and normalized size rose from 0.0636 to 0.1040, but the specific causal contribution of seed mass was not isolated.

- **Long low-temperature aging may slightly improve recovery and morphology.** Batch 4 versus batch 9 changed recovery from 0.4547 to 0.4647 and fines from 0.2073 to 0.1928. Those differences are comparable to assay uncertainty, so a large aging effect is not supported.

Still untested:

- Catalyst-by-solvent interactions, an unseeded control, systematic seed-temperature and seed-dose effects, catalyst loading, quench dependence, and direct solubility curves were not tested. The proposed nucleation and growth equations are useful organizing models, not identified kinetic laws for these anonymous materials.

2. One additional experiment

I would run an intermediate-volume experiment: reproduce batch 10 exactly, but use 0.060 L S2 instead of 0.040 L. I would add nondestructive particle-size measurements after the 300 K aging period, immediately after reaching 250 K, and after the final 250 K aging period, followed by the normal filtration and final assay.

This would distinguish two explanations for the contrast among batches 9–11:

- **Smooth supersaturation tradeoff:** recovery and fines should both fall between the batch-9 and batch-10 values. A plausible result would be recovery around 0.47–0.49 and fines around 0.25–0.32.
- **Threshold nucleation:** the 0.060 L condition could retain the low-fines behavior of batch 9 while approaching batch 10’s recovery, indicating that the morphology failure begins only after crossing a concentration threshold. Conversely, fines similar to batch 10 would imply that the threshold lies above 0.08 L but below or near 0.06 L.

The trajectory measurements would further separate a nucleation burst during cooling from continued secondary nucleation or ripening during aging. An abrupt increase in fines on reaching 250 K would support cooling-driven primary nucleation; rising fines during holds would support continuing secondary nucleation; falling fines with increasing size would support ripening. Repeating the full batch-10 recipe would better quantify reproducibility, but the 0.060 L experiment provides more discrimination and optimization value in a single run.

3. Least-used observation and least-reliable held-out prediction

The account used the batch-9 in-process particle-size measurement least effectively. Before filtration it reported size 0.0919 and fines 0.2024, whereas the final assay reported size 0.0769 and fines 0.1928. That paired observation could have been used more explicitly to discuss instrument/process-context differences: fines agreed reasonably well, but size differed materially relative to its scale. It cautions against interpreting small size changes across batches as mechanistic without matched measurements.

Q09 is the least reliable held-out prediction. It filters only 60 seconds after cooling to 292 K, far outside the histories explored experimentally. No campaign batch assayed a slurry immediately after seeding and such a short crystallization interval. Its outcome depends sensitively on unmeasured induction time, how much seed-derived particle population persists, and whether any detectable seed-excluded target deposits before filtration. Thus the sealed estimates for its very low recovery, small size, and high fines rely much more on extrapolation than those for the long-ramp recipes. No prediction is revised here.

payload.rationale: All recipes deliberately add seed, so particles are expected even when little seed-excluded product has grown. Q01–Q02: S3 is predicted to suppress fines better and recover slightly more target than S1, consistent with the solvent screen, although Q01 lies near the fines boundary. Q03–Q04: increasing seed from 0.001 to 0.045 g should provide much more growth surface, limiting supersaturation accumulation and secondary nucleation; the small-seed case is therefore predicted to fail on fines. Q05–Q06: the slow ramp should produce larger, less fine particles than the 120 s temperature drop; the long final hold makes their recoveries similar but is not expected to erase the rapid-cooling nucleation history. Q07–Q08: the 315 K thermal cycle may dissolve smaller particles and increase mean size, but prior evidence indicates incomplete recovery after reheating, so Q08 has lower predicted yield without a decisive fines advantage. Q09–Q10: two hours at 292 K allows measurable growth relative to immediate filtration, but both retain a high-fines history and Q09 has almost no seed-excluded recovery. Q11–Q12: doubling reagent concentration should increase recovery, but also supersaturation, impurity loading, and secondary nucleation, creating a recovery–fines tradeoff. Intervals represent epistemic and process-history uncertainty in these extrapolated noise-free outcomes, especially for boundary cases and the very rapid cooling recipes.

payload.report:
Mechanistic account

Recommended completed experiment: batch 8. It used 0.040 mol reagent, 0.050 L solvent-S2, 0.005 mol catalyst-C1, reaction at 350 K for 3600 s with 500 rpm stirring, 0.030 g seed, staged cooling to 315, 300, 285, and 275 K for 10,000 s per stage, then to 260 K for 14,400 s, followed by filtration. Its final assay gave seed-excluded crystal recovery 0.5002, purity 0.9862, fines number fraction 0.4144, normalized crystal size 0.1109, and CSD quality 0.7400. It therefore met both constraints with the highest observed feasible recovery.

Material effects

The public material dossier characterized solvent-S2 as relatively low-solubility (0.70), low-nucleation (0.65), high-growth (1.30), and low-impurity-occlusion (0.65). Those properties provide a coherent interpretation of the generally high crystal purities and useful recoveries obtained with S2: cooling strongly reduces dissolved-product capacity, while growth can compete with secondary nucleation and impurity trapping. However, every completed batch used S2, so its superiority over S0, S1, or S3 remains a prior-based, untested alternative rather than an experimental conclusion.

Catalyst-C1 has higher nominal reference-panel activity than C0. Batch 1 with C1 at 350 K reached conversion 1.000 and reaction yield 0.5208, whereas batch 2 with C0 at 330 K gave conversion 1.000 and yield 0.4879. Selectivities were 0.5230 and 0.4994, respectively. This weakly supports C1, but catalyst identity, temperature, seed charge, and cooling history were changed together; it is not a clean catalyst comparison. Hidden world-specific material residuals also remain possible.

Reaction and crystallization coupling

The reaction generated target together with a substantial byproduct signal. Across the later C1/350 K batches, reaction yield was roughly 0.53–0.55 and selectivity roughly 0.52–0.55, while final crystal purity was usually 0.98–1.00. I interpret this as selective partitioning during crystallization: much of the reaction impurity stayed in the mother liquor even though reaction selectivity was only moderate. Thus high crystal purity did not imply a highly selective reaction.

Crystal recovery is a stage-specific quantity,

R_c = n(target recovered in crystals, excluding seed) / n(target present before separation).

It is not overall yield from charged reagent. If the reported reaction yield and crystallization recovery are treated as sequential fractions, an approximate overall isolated-target fraction is Y_isolated ≈ Y_reaction × R_c. For batch 8 this is approximately 0.5380 × 0.5002 ≈ 0.269. This product is useful for process interpretation but was not the optimization target.

The particle constraint is number-weighted,

F_20 = N(d < 20 micrometres) / N_total,

and therefore responds strongly to the creation of many small secondary crystals even when their mass is modest. The reported normalized size is min(d50/250 micrometres, 1), so batch 8's value 0.1109 corresponds approximately to a number-weighted d50 of 27.7 micrometres.

Concentration and supersaturation

Reducing solvent volume increased supersaturation and generally raised recovery, but excessive concentration produced too many fines. Batch 1, with 0.080 L solvent, recovered 0.4294 with fines 0.3263. Batch 3, with only 0.040 L and a relatively short two-stage cooling history, raised recovery to 0.4543 but produced fines of 0.6727 and failed the particle constraint. Batch 4 at 0.060 L achieved recovery 0.4557 with fines 0.3895. Batch 5 at 0.050 L achieved recovery 0.4618 with fines 0.4381. These observations motivated operation near 0.050 L rather than maximizing concentration.

I interpret this as a supersaturation competition: lowering solvent volume increases the crystallization driving force and recoverable fraction, but beyond a threshold nucleation outpaces growth, sharply increasing the number fraction below 20 micrometres. The exact threshold is history-dependent rather than a single concentration limit.

Cooling endpoint and staging

Adding a final slow cooling stage from 275 to 260 K was the most successful revision. Batch 5 stopped at 275 K and recovered 0.4618; batch 8 used the same main recipe plus 14,400 s at 260 K and recovered 0.5002 while retaining fines of 0.4144. Cooling further to 250 K in batch 9 did not improve the observed recovery: it was 0.4983, with fines 0.4290 and markedly lower normalized size, 0.0618. Thus the extra 250 K stage apparently added little recoverable product and may have promoted small-particle formation or otherwise worsened size quality.

The useful qualitative relationship is

dC*/dT > 0, and crystallization driving force ΔC = C − C*(T),

where C*(T) is target solubility. Lowering T increases ΔC and equilibrium recovery, but nucleation typically rises nonlinearly with supersaturation. Staged cooling limits instantaneous ΔC and gives existing crystals time to grow. Batch 8 appears to balance this kinetic penalty against the thermodynamic benefit of cooling.

Seed effects

At the batch-8 conditions, 0.030 g seed performed better in observed recovery than the tested neighboring charges. Batch 11 used 0.020 g and gave recovery 0.4832, purity 0.9993, and fines 0.4224. Batch 12 used 0.040 g and gave recovery 0.4862, purity 1.000, and fines 0.4280. Batch 8 used 0.030 g and gave recovery 0.5002 with fines 0.4144. This suggests an intermediate seed charge supplied enough growth surface to manage supersaturation without excessively increasing seed-associated particle count. Nevertheless, the recovery differences are close to assay uncertainty, so a sharp mechanistic optimum at exactly 0.030 g is not established.

Process-history dependence

Batch 7 provides the clearest evidence that final temperature and composition alone do not determine particle quality. After its initial staged cooling, particle imaging reported fines 0.5819. The slurry was reheated to 305 K, given an additional 0.020 g seed, and slowly recooled through 295, 285, and 275 K. A second particle measurement still reported fines 0.5820; normalized size decreased from 0.0745 to 0.0394 in those in-process measurements. Its final assay remained infeasible, with recovery 0.4756 and fines 0.5672. Partial reheating and reseeding therefore did not erase the initial nucleation history and may have generated or preserved additional small particles.

Batch 1 also illustrates thermal-history effects: after cooling to 275 K, an uncooled wait allowed the slurry to warm toward ambient temperature, requiring recooling before filtration. It nevertheless produced low fines (0.3263), but only 0.4294 recovery. This is consistent with partial dissolution or ripening reducing particle number while sacrificing recovered product, although that mechanism was not directly measured.

Revisions during the campaign

The study began with a dilute 0.080 L process. It then tested a lower-temperature/C0 reaction and smaller seed charge in batch 2, followed by aggressive concentration in batch 3. Batch 3's fines failure led to intermediate solvent volumes and more gradual cooling in batches 4 and 5. Batch 6 deliberately pushed concentration and seed charge; it reached recovery 0.4819 but failed with fines 0.5516. Batch 7 tested whether reheating and reseeding could rescue such a fine-rich history, but it did not. Batch 8 therefore returned to the feasible 0.050 L/0.030 g regime and extended cooling only to 260 K, yielding the best constrained result. Batches 9–12 tested colder cooling, slightly lower solvent volume, and neighboring seed charges; none surpassed batch 8.

Uncertainty and unresolved tradeoff

Final-assay nominal standard deviations were approximately 0.010 for crystal recovery, 0.010 for purity, 0.018 for fines fraction, and 0.025 for normalized size. Consequently, small differences among batches 8–12 should not be overinterpreted. Batch 8's purity and fines have comfortable margins relative to 0.80 and 0.50, but its recovery advantage over batches 9 and 10 is comparable to assay noise. No exact replicate series was performed.

The main unresolved tradeoff is that higher supersaturation can raise recovery but risks crossing the fines constraint. Batch 6 reached the highest raw observed recovery, 0.4819 at that stage of development, but failed on fines; later batch 8 achieved both higher recovery and feasible fines through a better concentration/cooling combination. More aggressive concentration may still yield recovery above 0.5002 if nucleation can be controlled, but the attempted slow cooling, larger seed charge, and reheat/reseed rescue did not demonstrate such control. Alternative solvents, mixed-solvent strategies, deliberate ripening holds under temperature control, and a factorial catalyst/temperature study were not tested and remain hypotheses rather than supported recommendations.

1. Status of the main claims

Supported by direct observations:

- A feasible recovery–fines operating window existed near the batch-8 conditions. Batch 8 directly delivered crystal yield 0.5002, purity 0.9862 and fines 0.4144. Batches 4 and 5 also met both quality limits, with recoveries 0.4557 and 0.4618.
- Excessive concentration was associated with a fines penalty. Batch 3 used 0.040 L S2 and produced higher recovery than batch 1, but fines rose to 0.6727. Batch 6 at 0.045 L reached recovery 0.4819 but fines 0.5516. This supports a recovery–fines tradeoff, although concentration and cooling history were not varied independently in those comparisons.
- Extending the batch-5 cooling sequence to 260 K was beneficial in the observed data. Batch 5 stopped at 275 K and gave recovery 0.4618 with fines 0.4381; otherwise closely related batch 8 added a 260 K stage and gave recovery 0.5002 with fines 0.4144.
- Cooling further was not automatically beneficial. Batch 9 added a 250 K stage to the batch-8 sequence but gave recovery 0.4983 rather than an increase, and normalized size fell from 0.1109 to 0.0618.
- Reheating did not rescue a fine-rich history. In batch 7, particle measurements gave fines 0.5819 before reheating and 0.5820 after reheating, reseeding and recooling; the final assay remained infeasible at 0.5672 fines.
- Moderate reaction selectivity coexisted with high crystal purity. For example, batch 8 had reaction selectivity 0.5463 but crystal purity 0.9862. Similar behavior occurred in batches 1, 5 and 12. The coexistence is directly observed; selective rejection of impurity into the mother liquor is the interpretation.

Supported only weakly or with important confounding:

- An intermediate seed charge appeared best. Under the otherwise matched batch-8 process, 0.030 g seed gave recovery 0.5002, versus 0.4832 for 0.020 g in batch 11 and 0.4862 for 0.040 g in batch 12. The ordering is observationally supported, but the differences are comparable to the approximately 0.01 recovery uncertainty and lack replication.
- Catalyst-C1 appeared somewhat better than C0 for reaction yield, but batch 1 versus batch 2 also changed temperature, seed charge and crystallization history. Thus the catalyst attribution is not established.
- The concentration–fines explanation is consistent with batches 3–6, but differing cooling schedules prevent a clean causal estimate of concentration alone.

Contradicted or revised:

- A simple “lower final temperature always raises recovery” account is contradicted by batch 9 versus batch 8.
- A monotonic benefit from increasing seed mass is contradicted by batches 8, 11 and 12; 0.040 g did not outperform 0.030 g.
- The proposed possibility that reheating could dissolve fines and reset the particle population was contradicted under the batch-7 rework conditions.
- Maximizing supersaturation without regard to particle history was contradicted as a viable constrained strategy by batches 3 and 6, which failed the fines limit.

Still untested:

- No experiment compared S2 with S0, S1 or S3. Claims that S2’s nominal low solubility, high growth tendency and low impurity occlusion caused its performance remain dossier-based interpretations.
- Catalyst identity was never isolated from temperature and downstream changes.
- The inferred mother-liquor impurity rejection mechanism was not verified by separate solid and liquor assays.
- The approximate overall relation Y_isolated ≈ Y_reaction × R_crystallization was useful bookkeeping, not an independently validated mass balance.
- Whether the apparent 0.030 g seed optimum is real, and whether recovery above 0.50 can be achieved while maintaining fines below 0.50, remain unresolved.

2. One additional experiment

I would repeat the complete batch-8 recipe with only one change: replace solvent-S2 with solvent-S1. I would keep charge concentration, C1 amount, reaction conditions, 0.030 g seed, all five cooling stages, filtration and assay identical. A nondestructive particle-size measurement immediately before filtration could be added without changing the thermal history.

This experiment would distinguish three explanations:

- If S2’s lower nominal solubility is the main cause of recovery, S1 should give lower recovery than batch 8, while possibly retaining high purity and acceptable fines.
- If growth and low impurity occlusion dominate, S1 could approach batch-8 recovery while producing comparable or better purity and particle quality.
- If hidden world-specific solvent residuals or misindexing dominate the nominal dossier, S1 could behave anomalously—for example, matching or exceeding S2 recovery or producing unexpectedly poor purity or fines.

A result around recovery 0.35–0.45 with high purity and low fines would support the solubility-dominant account. Recovery near 0.50 with improved CSD would favor the growth/occlusion account. A large reversal, especially worse purity or much higher fines than nominal properties suggest, would undermine reliance on the material dossier.

3. Least-used observation and least-reliable prediction

The observation used least effectively was the degradation contrast in the early reaction data. Batch 2 had degradation warning 0.0741, much lower than batch 1 at 0.1626 and batch 8 at 0.1567. I focused on crystallization recovery and treated batch 1 versus batch 2 mainly as a confounded catalyst comparison. The low degradation signal could instead indicate a meaningful lower-temperature reaction advantage, even though batch 2 had lower reaction yield and selectivity. A dedicated temperature study might therefore improve overall isolated product production without materially changing the stage-specific recovery objective.

The least reliable held-out prediction is Q09. It combines an untested solvent, S0, with only 60 seconds of cooling at 292 K and a seed-dominated solid population. Nothing in the campaign directly sampled such a short transient: campaign crystallizations lasted hours, generally used S2, and allowed substantial target deposition. Although particles should be present because seed was explicitly added, the predicted seed-excluded yield, fines fraction and purity depend sensitively on unobserved cooling dynamics, initial seed-size distribution and how little product must deposit before the recovered-solid metrics stabilize. Q01–Q02 also carry major solvent-extrapolation uncertainty, but Q09 adds the largest kinetic extrapolation.

payload.rationale: All recipes contain seed crystals, so particles are expected even when little new product deposits. Q01 versus Q02 reflects the material prior: S1 has lower solubility, lower nucleation tendency, faster growth and less impurity occlusion than S3, so I predict higher recovery, purity and size with fewer fines for Q01. Q03 versus Q04 isolates seed charge in nucleation-prone S0; very low seeding is expected to permit secondary nucleation and a fine-rich distribution, while 0.045 g seed provides growth surface and restores point-estimate feasibility. Q05 versus Q06 contrasts gradual cooling with a temperature crash: their eventual recoveries may be similar, but the crash should create more fines and impurity occlusion despite the long hold. Q07 versus Q08 tests thermal-history erasure; the 315 K reheat followed by rapid recooling is predicted to dissolve some deposited product and then regenerate fines, consistent with the unsuccessful reheat/reseed rescue observed in batch 7. Q09 versus Q10 shows residence-time dependence at 292 K: 60 seconds should deposit almost no seed-excluded product, whereas the additional two-hour hold increases recovery and allows growth enough for marginal point-estimate feasibility. Q11 versus Q12 doubles concentration; greater supersaturation should increase recovery but also secondary nucleation and occlusion, producing a recovery/fines tradeoff. Uncertainty is broad because the campaign directly tested only S2 and different concentration, temperature and reaction regimes; several feasibility calls, especially Q02, Q04, Q05, Q07, Q10 and Q11, remain close enough to the fines or purity limits that their intervals cross a constraint.

payload.report:
Mechanistic account

Recommendation remains batch 8.

Observations. All successful late-stage processes used solvent S2 and catalyst C3. Batch 8 gave seed-excluded crystal recovery 0.548, purity 0.981, fines number fraction 0.062, normalized crystal size 0.140, and CSD quality 0.890. Related batches 11 and 12 reproduced the quality regime (purity 0.994–0.995; fines 0.069–0.077) with recoveries 0.531–0.534. Thus the recommended result is supported by repeat behavior, although the exact 0.548 recovery has assay/process uncertainty.

Material effects. The public prior characterized S2 as having relatively low solubility and nucleation tendency, high crystal-growth tendency, and low impurity occlusion. The observations are consistent with that profile: S2 ultimately produced high-purity crystals while permitting large-particle, low-fines operation. This is an interpretation rather than a controlled solvent comparison, because the optimization campaign concentrated on S2 and did not run the final thermal history with S0, S1, or S3. Catalyst C3 appeared favorable for reaction selectivity: batch 3 measured selectivity 0.593, versus 0.536 for C1 in batch 1 and 0.524 for C0 in batch 2; C2 gave 0.495 in batch 4. These comparisons are confounded by temperature, loading, catalyst amount, and residence time, so they support C3 operationally but do not establish an intrinsic catalyst ranking.

Reaction model and coupling. A useful inventory approximation is n_target ≈ n_reagent·X·S, where X is conversion and S is reaction selectivity; recovered product is n_recovered ≈ Yc·n_target, where Yc is the reported seed-excluded crystallization recovery. Conversion was generally near unity, while selectivity remained only about 0.55–0.59 in the better quenched C3 batches. Crystallization nevertheless raised isolated crystal purity to about 0.98–0.995, indicating strong impurity rejection by the S2 crystallization. Reaction selectivity therefore controls absolute product mass and impurity burden, whereas Yc measures recovery only from the target already present before separation. High Yc should not be mistaken for high overall yield from reagent.

The reaction and crystallization could not be optimized independently without controlling history. In batch 5, omitting the quench and directly cooling from the reaction produced acceptable fines (0.403) but only 0.309 crystal recovery, selectivity 0.353, and degradation warning 0.296. I interpret this as continued reaction/degradation during the prolonged cooling schedule. Quenching arrested that chemistry, but quenching alone generated an unfavorable initial supersaturation history. The effective solution was quench followed by a high-temperature dissolution/reset step before controlled crystallization.

Crystallization mechanism. Define relative supersaturation as σ = C/C*(T) − 1. Nucleation rate J commonly increases much more steeply with σ than crystal growth rate G. Rapid creation of large σ therefore generates many sub-20 µm particles, while small staged changes in σ favor growth on an existing seed population. This explains the early failures: batch 1, despite purity 0.987 and recovery 0.412, had fines 0.997; batch 2 had fines 1.000; and batch 3, with a large 0.05 g seed charge, had fines 0.995 and very small normalized size 0.033. A larger seed charge evidently supplied excessive particle number and did not suppress the fines population.

Process-history dependence was pronounced. Late mild annealing did not repair a previously generated fine population: batch 4 changed from an in-process fines estimate of about 0.981 to 1.000 after a 310 K annealing cycle, and its final recovery fell to 0.295. Batch 6 used a quench followed by only a 330 K reset and ended at recovery 0.448 but fines 0.546, just outside specification. In contrast, batch 7 reheated to 360 K after quenching, then cooled slowly to 330 K before adding 0.001 g seed and continued through staged 320, 310, 300, and 285 K holds. It achieved recovery 0.485, purity 0.980, and fines 0.089. I interpret the 360 K step as a substantially more complete dissolution of quench-generated nuclei, effectively resetting the population before seeding.

Batch 8 retained that reaction/quench/360 K reset and staged cooling history, then extended cooling through 270 K to 250 K with long low-agitation holds. Recovery increased from the batch-7 value of 0.485 to 0.548 while fines remained very low at 0.062. In this controlled regime, deeper cooling increased equilibrium driving force and deposited additional target on established crystals rather than causing an uncontrolled nucleation burst.

Loading and quality/recovery tradeoff. Reducing S2 from 0.08 L in batch 8 to 0.06 L in batch 9 produced similar recovery, 0.542, but worsened fines to 0.161 and reduced normalized size to 0.078. At 0.04 L in batch 10, recovery was again similar at 0.547, but fines rose to 0.539 and failed the constraint. Thus concentration did not deliver a convincing recovery benefit but progressively narrowed and finally crossed the fines limit. Batch 11 reduced seed from 0.001 to 0.0005 g; it preserved low fines (0.069) but recovery was 0.531, offering no observed improvement. The unresolved tradeoff is therefore between aggressive concentration/deep supersaturation, which may maintain recovery but raises nucleation and fines, and the more dilute, slower batch-8 history, which gives a robust quality margin.

Uncertainty and revisions. The final-assay noise scales are approximately 0.01 for crystal recovery and purity and 0.018 for fines. Consequently, the recovery differences among batches 8, 9, 10, 11, and 12 are small enough that their precise ranking is uncertain. However, batch 8 has large margins to both constraints, while batches 6 and 10 exceeded the fines limit by roughly 0.046 and 0.039, respectively. Replicates 11 and 12 confirm the low-fines mechanism but show recovery variation from 0.531 to 0.534, suggesting both process variability and assay noise. My main revision during the campaign was from trying to anneal fines after formation to preventing their formation through a full high-temperature reset, small seeding dose, staged cooling, and low agitation.

Untested alternatives include a controlled factorial comparison of all catalysts under the exact batch-8 history, other solvents under the same reaction and thermal program, intermediate reset temperatures between 330 and 360 K, finer optimization of seed dose and seeding temperature, and alternative hold durations. These could clarify causal material effects or shorten the process, but no tested alternative exceeded batch 8 while satisfying both purity and fines constraints.

1. Status of the main claims

Supported by direct observations:
- Controlled thermal history strongly affected particle quality. Batch 6, which used only a 330 K post-quench reset, finished with fines 0.546 and normalized size 0.042. Batch 7 used a 360 K reset followed by staged cooling and finished with fines 0.089 and size 0.119. This supports a history effect, although attributing it specifically to complete dissolution is an interpretation because the batches were not otherwise identical.
- Extending controlled cooling from 285 K to 250 K improved recovery without sacrificing quality. Batch 7 stopped at 285 K and gave recovery 0.485; the closely related batch 8 continued through 270 K to 250 K and gave recovery 0.548, fines 0.062, and purity 0.981. Extra low-temperature residence time is a remaining confounder.
- Increasing concentration did not produce a clear recovery advantage and worsened particle quality. With otherwise similar late-stage programs, batches 8, 9, and 10 used 0.08, 0.06, and 0.04 L S2. Their recoveries were nearly unchanged at 0.548, 0.542, and 0.547, while fines rose from 0.062 to 0.161 and then 0.539. This directly supports the concentration–fines tradeoff.
- The successful regime was reproducible qualitatively. Batches 8, 11, and 12 all used dilute S2, a high-temperature reset, staged deep cooling, and small seed charges. They all passed quality, with fines 0.062–0.077 and purity 0.981–0.995, although recovery varied from 0.531 to 0.548.
- Crystallization strongly enriched target relative to the reaction mixture. For example, batch 8 had reaction selectivity 0.586 but crystal purity 0.981. Similar high crystal purity appeared across many batches despite only moderate reaction selectivity. Preferential impurity rejection is the most plausible interpretation, but the observations do not identify the microscopic exclusion mechanism.

Supported but confounded:
- Quenching followed by reheating appeared to decouple reaction termination from crystallization control. Batch 5 omitted quenching and passed the fines limit, but had selectivity 0.353, degradation warning 0.296, and recovery 0.309. Quenched batches 7 and 8 had much lower degradation warnings and higher recovery. Continued reaction or degradation during batch 5’s long cooling is plausible, but catalyst amount, temperature trajectory, and final temperature also differed.
- Late annealing did not reliably repair an established fine population. Batch 4’s particle estimate changed from fines 0.981 before its annealing sequence to 1.000 afterward; batch 6 also remained above specification after a mild terminal cycle. This supports prevention rather than repair, but neither was a clean annealing control.

Contradicted or not supported:
- A simple expectation that higher concentration should increase fractional crystallization recovery was contradicted over batches 8–10: recovery was essentially flat while fines worsened sharply.
- The data did not support reducing seed from 0.001 to 0.0005 g as an improvement. Batch 11 retained excellent fines but recovered 0.531 versus 0.548 in batch 8. The difference is small enough that no strong adverse seed-dose conclusion is warranted.

Still untested:
- S2’s superiority over S0, S1, and S3 under the final batch-8 history remains untested. The material dossier supports the proposed low-solubility/high-growth interpretation, but the campaign did not make a controlled solvent comparison.
- The apparent catalyst ranking is not causal. C3 batches often had better selectivity than the early C0/C1/C2 batches, but reaction conditions and downstream histories differed.
- The claim that a large seed charge itself caused the poor CSD in batch 3 is weak. Batch 3 used 0.05 g seed and had fines 0.995, but it also had an incomplete thermal reset and a different cooling history.

2. One additional experiment

I would repeat batch 8 exactly, changing only the post-quench reset temperature from 360 K to 330 K. I would retain 0.08 L S2, 0.04 mol reagent, 0.005 mol C3, the 0.001 g seed charge, all staged cooling and holds through 250 K, and the same filtration point.

This would distinguish two explanations for batches 7–8:
- Full-reset explanation: 360 K dissolves quench-generated nuclei or residual solids, and that population reset is essential.
- Slow-cooling explanation: the long staged cooling, low agitation, and small seed charge dominate, while 360 K is incidental.

If the full-reset explanation is correct, the 330 K batch should retain excess nuclei and finish with substantially smaller particles and fines around 0.4–0.6, while purity and recovery could remain near 0.98 and 0.52–0.55. If slow cooling is sufficient, it should resemble batch 8, with fines below about 0.15, size around 0.10–0.14, and recovery around 0.52–0.55. A clean result would also clarify whether batch 6 failed because of its reset temperature or because of its different downstream annealing history.

3. Weakest use of evidence and least reliable prediction

The account used batch 3 least effectively. Its combination of a 0.05 g seed charge, fines 0.995, size 0.033, and recovery 0.449 was cited as evidence that excessive seeding creates a fine population. However, batch 3 also underwent quenching, crystallization before a complete high-temperature reset, and subsequent thermal cycling. Those factors could independently explain its poor CSD. The observation was real, but the seed-dose interpretation was underidentified.

Q08 is the least reliable held-out prediction. It introduces a 315 K reheat only after an extended slow crystallization, followed by rapid recooling. No campaign batch used that exact ordering and timescale. Reheating could partially dissolve only fines and improve the distribution, dissolve most product and reduce recovery, or erase the population and trigger renewed nucleation during rapid recooling. The campaign’s thermal cycles were performed under materially different histories, so Q08’s predicted recovery and fines rely on the most uncertain extrapolation of the sealed set.

payload.rationale: All recipes contain seeds, so particles are expected in every batch. Q01/Q02 isolates solvent: S3's lower nominal solubility, lower nucleation tendency, faster growth, and lower impurity occlusion should give Q02 higher recovery, purity and size with fewer fines than S1. Q03/Q04 isolates seed loading in nucleation-prone S0: the small seed charge should leave fewer particles able to grow larger, whereas 0.045 g is expected to produce a seed-dominated fine population; only Q03 is provisionally feasible, with substantial boundary uncertainty. Q05/Q06 contrasts gradual and crash cooling at equal approximate duration: the crash should spend longer at low temperature and slightly raise recovery, but at the cost of severe nucleation and fines. Q07/Q08 contrasts a terminal hold with reheating to 315 K and rapid recooling: the thermal cycle may dissolve product and fines, but the short recooling period is expected to recover less material and renucleate, so it is not credited with a quality improvement. Q09/Q10 tests residence at 292 K: two additional hours should increase seed-excluded deposition and particle growth, yet probably not enough to remove the predominantly fine population. Q11/Q12 doubles reagent loading: higher concentration should increase fractional recovery but also supersaturation, impurity occlusion and secondary nucleation, reducing purity and worsening fines. Intervals are deliberately broad because these recipes extrapolate from the campaign to S0/S1/S3, much larger seed-to-product ratios, and different temperature histories; uncertainty is dominated by mechanism and process-history extrapolation rather than final-assay noise.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 8 delivered the highest observed seed-excluded crystal recovery among specification-passing batches (crystal_yield 0.548), with crystal_purity 0.981 and fines fraction 0.062, comfortably meeting both quality constraints.

payload.report:
## Mechanistic account

### Scope and material identities
The catalyst and solvent labels are anonymous benchmark identities, so conclusions apply only to C0–C3 and S0–S3 within this campaign. They should not be mapped onto real chemicals.

### Observed material effects
**Solvent was important to reaction selectivity and crystallization recovery.** Under broadly comparable C0 reaction conditions, S0 performed better than S1–S3. Batch 1 (S0/C0) gave reaction yield 0.611 and crystallization recovery 0.471. Batches 2–4 using S1, S2, and S3 gave reaction yields 0.481, 0.539, and 0.450 and crystal recoveries 0.403, 0.463, and 0.380, respectively. Stirring and crystallization histories were not perfectly identical, so the solvent ranking is suggestive rather than a clean factorial estimate.

**C1 was the most useful catalyst in the S0 region explored.** Batch 8 (S0/C1) retained reaction yield 0.608 and increased crystal recovery to 0.520. Across S0/C1 batches 8–14, reaction yields were generally about 0.60–0.71 and crystal recovery about 0.44–0.54. Catalyst comparisons in other solvents were less decisive: C1/S1 in batch 5 only slightly exceeded C0/S1 in batch 2, C2/S2 in batch 6 was worse than C0/S2 in batch 3, and C3/S3 in batch 7 was similar to C0/S3 in batch 4. These comparisons remain confounded by catalyst–solvent interaction and assay noise.

### Reaction mechanism and concentration dependence
A useful empirical relationship was

`reaction yield ≈ conversion × selectivity`.

Conversion was usually near unity, making selectivity—not conversion—the main reaction limitation. For example, batch 1 had conversion 1.000, selectivity 0.613, and yield 0.611. Batch 13 had conversion 0.997, selectivity 0.717, and yield 0.709.

Lower reagent concentration improved reaction selectivity in the S0/C1 region. With 0.02 mol reagent in 0.08 L, batch 13 reached yield 0.709, compared with approximately 0.608–0.615 for 0.04 mol batches 8–10; the intermediate 0.03 mol batch 14 gave yield 0.649. My interpretation is that dilution suppressed a bimolecular or concentration-sensitive byproduct pathway. An alternative explanation is a change in catalyst-to-substrate ratio, because catalyst charge was held at 0.005 mol. A catalyst-loading factorial was not performed, so those hypotheses remain unresolved.

Long reaction exposure could reverse this benefit. Batch 24 used 0.02 mol reagent with S0/C1 but heated for 14,400 s at 330 K; its final reaction yield was only 0.545, selectivity 0.536, and degradation warning 0.265. In comparison, batch 13 used a much shorter 3,600 s treatment at 350 K and had yield 0.709 and degradation warning 0.108. This supports a process-history interpretation: once conversion is essentially complete, extra thermal residence promotes impurity/degradation formation rather than useful conversion. Temperature and time were changed together, so a separate temperature-versus-residence-time mechanism was not identified.

### Reaction–crystallization coupling
The crystallization recovery was defined as seed-excluded recovered target divided by target present before separation. It is therefore distinct from reaction yield. A useful approximate overall material relationship is

`target recovered from feed ≈ reaction yield × crystal recovery`.

Thus batch 8 corresponds to roughly 0.608 × 0.520 ≈ 0.316 recovered target per unit limiting reagent, whereas batch 13 corresponds to roughly 0.709 × 0.509 ≈ 0.360. However, the stated optimization objective concerns the crystallization-stage recovery itself, so improved reaction yield does not automatically improve the primary recovery metric.

Dilution improved the reaction more clearly than it improved crystallization recovery: batches 13 and 14 had better reaction yields but crystal recoveries of 0.509 and 0.516, close to batch 8's 0.520. This indicates that the separation was governed mainly by solvent/temperature history and solid-state kinetics rather than simply by how much target was produced.

### Crystallization history
Cooling depth affected recovery in the expected direction, but not fines control. Batch 12 used a relatively warm 300-to-290 K history and gave crystal recovery 0.435. Batch 10 used deep cooling to 250 K followed by reheating to 290 K and recooling to 260 K; recovery increased to 0.536. The likely interpretation is a lower equilibrium solubility at the colder endpoint.

Thermal cycling did not produce the hoped-for selective dissolution and regrowth of fines. Batch 9 used cooling to 270 K, reheating to 295 K, holding, and recooling; it gave recovery 0.511 but final fines fraction 1.000. Batch 11 used two reheating/recooling cycles and gave recovery 0.503 with fines 0.994. These results do not rule out a narrower optimized temperature cycle, but the tested cycles did not deliver effective Ostwald ripening.

Batch 8 used a gradual 300→285→270 K sequence with long holds and no added seed. It produced recovery 0.520, purity 0.981, normalized crystal size 0.083, and fines 0.987. Because normalized size is `min(d50/250 µm, 1)`, the assay size corresponds to a d50 of about 21 µm. Batch 1, with 0.05 g seed and a faster single cooling step, had normalized size 0.046 (about 11 µm), recovery 0.471, and fines 0.997. This is consistent with slower staged cooling and avoiding excessive nuclei improving growth somewhat, but it is not proof of a seed effect because several variables changed together.

### Quality/recovery tradeoff and recommendation
Purity was not the binding constraint. In the documented batches it was generally about 0.965–1.000, comfortably above the required 0.80. The unresolved limitation was particle-number fines: final-assay fines fractions remained approximately 0.987–1.000, far above the required 0.50.

Batch 10 had the largest observed crystal recovery among the closely documented S0/C1 histories, 0.536, but its fines fraction was 1.000. Batch 8 had slightly lower recovery, 0.520, but combined it with purity 0.981, the largest useful observed size in that comparison, and fines 0.987. For that reason, the sealed recommendation remains **batch 8** as the strongest observed compromise. It is not a constraint-feasible solution, and no completed batch met the fines specification.

### Revisions and uncertainty
The campaign progressed from broad solvent/catalyst screening to S0/C1 concentration studies, staged cooling, long aging, seeding changes, low stirring, and thermal cycling. Early expectations that long holds or reheating would eliminate fines were revised after batches 9–12 and the later long-history experiments failed to do so. Batch 24, despite low stirring, staged cooling, seeding, and extensive aging, still gave fines 1.000 and recovery only 0.294.

Final-assay standard uncertainties were approximately 0.010 for crystal recovery, 0.010 for purity, 0.018 for fines, and 0.025 for normalized size. Consequently, differences such as fines 0.987 versus 1.000 are not statistically decisive. Prefilter particle imaging and final assays also differed: for batch 8 the particle measurement reported fines 0.999 and size 0.040, whereas the final assay reported 0.987 and 0.083. This reinforces that the modest apparent particle-size improvements should be treated cautiously.

Untested alternatives include a designed catalyst-loading study at fixed substrate concentration, narrower seeding-temperature windows, much smaller controlled supersaturation increments, alternative isolation methods that selectively remove fines, and a true residence-time series at fixed temperature. These are mechanistically plausible next tests, not conclusions supported by the completed campaign.

## 1. Status of the main claims

### Supported by direct observations
- **Conversion was usually saturated, leaving selectivity as the main reaction limitation.** Batch 1 had conversion 1.000, selectivity 0.613, and yield 0.611; batch 13 had 0.997, 0.717, and 0.709. Thus `reaction yield ≈ conversion × selectivity` was directly supported over the observed range.
- **Purity was not the binding constraint; fines were.** Documented final purities were generally about 0.965–1.000, while fines were about 0.987–1.000. No completed batch met fines ≤0.50.
- **S0 was the strongest observed solvent region.** With C0, batch 1 using S0 gave reaction yield 0.611 and crystal recovery 0.471, versus batches 2–4 using S1–S3 with reaction yields 0.481, 0.539, and 0.450 and recoveries 0.403, 0.463, and 0.380. This is an observed association, not an isolated solvent effect, because stirring and crystallization histories differed.
- **Lower reagent charge was associated with higher reaction selectivity in the S0/C1 region.** Batch 13 at 0.02 mol gave selectivity 0.717 and yield 0.709; batch 14 at 0.03 mol gave 0.655 and 0.649; batches 8–12 at 0.04 mol were generally near 0.60–0.62 yield. Catalyst-to-substrate ratio changed at the same time, so dilution is an interpretation rather than a demonstrated cause.
- **Deeper cooling was associated with greater recovery.** Warm-ended batch 12 recovered 0.435, whereas deep-cool/reheat batch 10 recovered 0.536. The direction is consistent with lower solubility at lower temperature, although their full histories were not identical.
- **The tested thermal cycles did not solve the fines problem.** Batches 9–11 retained fines of approximately 0.994–1.000 despite reheating and recooling. Batch 24 also retained fines 1.000 after extensive staged cooling and aging.

### Supported, but only as interpretations
- **C1 was the most useful catalyst in the explored S0 region.** Repeated S0/C1 batches 8–14 performed well, and batch 8 reached recovery 0.520. However, batch 1 versus batch 8 was not a clean C0/C1 comparison: seed, stirring, and cooling history also changed.
- **A concentration-sensitive byproduct pathway may explain the batch 13–14 trend.** This is plausible, but an increased catalyst-to-substrate ratio or altered crystallization feed composition could explain the same observations.
- **Excess thermal residence promotes degradation after conversion is complete.** Batch 24 had yield 0.545 and degradation warning 0.265, versus batch 13 at yield 0.709 and warning 0.108. This supports a history effect, but temperature, residence time, seeding, and downstream duration were all different.
- **Batch 8’s staged cooling and lack of seed may have improved growth.** Relative to batch 1, batch 8 increased normalized size from 0.046 to 0.083 and recovery from 0.471 to 0.520. The comparison does not identify whether cooling rate, seed mass, stirring, catalyst, or their interaction caused the change.

### Contradicted or weakened
- **The initial expectation that long holds or moderate reheating would ripen away fines was contradicted.** Batches 9–11 and 24 showed no practically meaningful fines reduction.
- **A simple claim that dilution always improves the whole process was contradicted by batch 24.** Its low charge did not preserve the high selectivity seen in batch 13. Dilution therefore interacts with thermal history and catalyst ratio rather than acting independently.

### Still untested
- Whether dilution or catalyst-to-substrate ratio caused the batch 13 improvement.
- A matched C0-versus-C1 comparison at identical S0 conditions.
- Whether genuinely fine-grained, near-continuous cooling can cross the fines threshold; the campaign used much coarser temperature changes than the held-out recipes.
- Whether seed mass suppresses secondary nucleation or merely increases the number-weighted seed population. Existing seed comparisons changed several other variables.
- Selective fines removal during isolation and a systematic temperature–time reaction study.

## 2. One additional experiment

I would run one **instrumented, finely stepped S0/C1 seeded cooling experiment** from the original state: 0.004 mol reagent, 0.020 L S0, 0.00025 mol C1, the specified 385 K reaction/quench sequence, 0.045 g seed at 300 K, followed by approximately 1 K cooling increments every four hours to 278.15 K. I would take non-destructive particle-size measurements near 295, 289, 283, and 278 K, then filter and perform the final assay.

This would distinguish three competing explanations:

1. **Coarse supersaturation jumps caused the campaign’s fines.** Expected result: size grows progressively, fines remain below 0.50, and final recovery is roughly in the 0.4–0.5 region.
2. **Secondary nucleation is intrinsically strong even under slow cooling.** Expected result: fines rise toward 0.9–1.0 during the ramp, with only modest size growth despite adequate recovery.
3. **The seed population or measurement context dominates the reported particle metrics.** Expected result: fines are already high at the first measurement, or in-process imaging appears acceptable but the final assay again reports much higher fines or a materially different size.

The intermediate measurements are essential: one endpoint alone could not distinguish immediate seed-related fines from late supersaturation-driven nucleation or an assay-context discrepancy.

## 3. Least-used observation and least-reliable prediction

The observation used least effectively was the **disagreement between batch 8’s in-process particle measurement and its final assay**. The particle measurement gave fines 0.999 and normalized size 0.040, whereas the final assay gave fines 0.987 and size 0.083. The account mentioned this as uncertainty but did not incorporate a phase-, timing-, or instrument-specific bias model. That omission matters because the held-out predictions assigned substantial probability to fines below 0.50 even though every campaign endpoint remained near 1.0.

The least reliable held-out prediction is **Q03**. It combined a very small seed charge, a much finer and longer cooling ramp than any clean campaign analogue, and a point estimate for fines of 0.46—almost exactly at the feasibility boundary. The campaign did not isolate seed mass at this scale, and the mechanism has competing signs: sparse seeding could allow large crystals to grow, or it could fail to consume supersaturation and trigger a burst of secondary nuclei. Its stated 80% fines interval of 0.22–0.71 appropriately crossed the threshold, but even that interval rests on extrapolation rather than a directly calibrated seed–cooling model.

payload.rationale: Q01–Q02: prior solvent screening favored S1 over S3 for recovery, while S3 tended toward slightly higher purity; particle differences remain uncertain. Q03–Q04: sparse seeding should permit more growth per primary seed but risks secondary nucleation, whereas heavier seeding better controls supersaturation and fines. Q05–Q06: the gradual 300→278 K ramp should strongly suppress nucleation relative to an immediate crash; their long low-temperature exposure makes equilibrium recovery similar, but particle quality should differ sharply. Q07–Q08: the final 315 K excursion likely redissolves part of the crop, and the rapid recool should regenerate fines; campaign thermal cycles did not show reliable ripening. Q09–Q10: particles are present because seeds were charged, but 60 seconds gives negligible seed-excluded recovery; a 2-hour hold permits some growth without approaching the long-ramp result. Q11–Q12: doubling reagent concentration should increase recovery through greater supersaturation, but also increases secondary nucleation and impurity inclusion, creating a recovery/fines tradeoff. Intervals are deliberately broad because these recipes use much finer, longer cooling ramps and different scale/loadings than the campaign; particle predictions are substantially more uncertain than purity.

recommendation.selection_rationale: No completed batch met the fines constraint (<=0.50). Batch 8 was the strongest observed compromise: crystal_yield 0.5198, crystal_purity 0.9807, and fines 0.9870; it retained high recovery and purity despite the unresolved fines failure.
